title: THE ROLE OF SPATIAL REFERENCE FRAMES IN ARCHITECTURE Misalignment Impairs Way-Finding Performance
research_question: Does the misalignment of local, cognitive reference frames, suggested by architectural features, lead to way-finding problems and impair the integration of spatial knowledge?

participants.description: College students (M = 20.6 years, range 18-48 years), 28 female, 28 male, from University of Idaho.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four synthetic, computer-generated office-building environments (single floor, ~54 offices), modeled in 3D Studio Max R3 and displayed via Cortona VRML client. Environments varied in 'alignment' (central elevator region aligned vs. misaligned by 45° with rest of building) and 'corners' (clipped vs. orthogonal). Textures were identical across environments. Five colored spheres on pedestals served as target objects, and a textured circle marked a central elevator location.

measures.instrument: Time to reach target objects in virtual environment (seconds)

measures.construct: Global configural spatial knowledge / Pointing accuracy
measures.instrument: Absolute pointing error (degrees) with a joystick to target objects from two fixed locations (elevator, hallway intersection) in four imagined orientations.
Selection and ranking of 16 schematic floor plans (including correct and distractors) that best depicted the experienced environment.

findings.antecedent: Alignment of central building part (aligned vs. misaligned)
findings.mechanism: Misalignment of local reference frames impairs integration of spatial knowledge, increasing cognitive workload.
findings.quote: the factor alignment showed a significant influence on way-finding times, F(1,51)=4.68, p = .035.

findings.antecedent: Alignment of central building part (aligned vs. misaligned)
findings.mechanism: Misalignment of local reference frames makes spatial knowledge integration more difficult.
findings.quote: Average way-finding times in the two aligned conditions were considerably lower (M = 35.8 s, SD = 15.6 s) than in the two misaligned conditions (M = 46.2 s, SD = 30.7 s).
The factor corners showed no reliable effect, F(1, 51) = 1.57, p = .215.
The interaction between alignment and corners was not significant, F < 1.

findings.antecedent: Alignment of central building part (aligned vs. misaligned) when pointing from elevator location
findings.mechanism: Misaligned local reference frames make it harder to orient oneself and integrate spatial knowledge, leading to higher pointing error.
findings.quote: The factor alignment had a significant effect on pointing accuracy for pointing judgments from the elevator, F(1,49) = 14.31, p < .001

findings.antecedent: Alignment of central building part (aligned vs. misaligned) when pointing from elevator location
findings.mechanism: Misalignment of local reference frames makes it harder to orient oneself and integrate spatial knowledge, leading to higher pointing error.
findings.quote: accuracy was better in the aligned case (M = 30.8°, SD = 13.2° ) than in the misaligned situation (M = 54.7°, SD = 30.5°).

findings.antecedent: Alignment of central building part (aligned vs. misaligned) when pointing from other hallway location
findings.mechanism: The advantage for aligned conditions was reduced to a nonsignificant difference when pointing from the second location, which mainly consisted of judgments within the same reference frame.
findings.quote: was not significant for pointing judgments from the other hallway F(1,51)=2.37, p=.130.

findings.antecedent: Corner type (clipped vs. orthogonal) when pointing from elevator location
findings.quote: No other main effects or interactions reached significance (F's < 1

findings.antecedent: Corner type (clipped vs. orthogonal) when pointing from other hallway location
findings.quote: No other main effects or interactions reached significance (F's < 1

findings.antecedent: Interaction between alignment and corner type when pointing from other hallway location
findings.quote: except the alignment × corner interaction for pointing judgments from the hallway, F[1,51]=3.11, p = .084.

findings.antecedent: Experienced environment (any of the four floor plans)
findings.consequent: Accuracy in identifying correct floor plan from 16 options (top choice)
findings.mechanism: Difficulty of matching immersive spatial experience to 2D representation, and homogenous set of targets/distractors.
findings.quote: The four groups did not differ significantly in their absolute accuracy in identifying the correct floor plan that they had encountered—neither as their top choice (range = 3 to 4 participants who chose the correct plan per group) nor as one of their top four choices (range = 5 to 8 participants per group), x² < 1.46, p > .5.

findings.consequent: Preference for aligned vs. misaligned floor plans (top choice)
findings.mechanism: Participants did not attend to this feature of the plan consciously.
findings.quote: Participants only minimally preferred aligned plans to misaligned plans. ... This difference in selection was not significant.

findings.antecedent: Experienced environment with original clipped corners
findings.consequent: Preference to select floor plans with clipped corners (top choice)
findings.mechanism: Participants showed a strong preference for the corner type they experienced.
findings.quote: Participants who had experienced the environment with the original clipped corners showed a strong preference to select floor plans that were clipped (25:3 for top choices, 96:16 for total choices)... significant, x² =7.38, p = .007 for top choices

findings.antecedent: Experienced environment with modified orthogonal floor plans
findings.consequent: Preference to select floor plans with orthogonal corners (top choice)
findings.mechanism: Participants did not discriminate strongly along this dimension.
findings.quote: whereas participants who had experienced the modified orthogonal floor plans did not discriminate strongly along this dimension (16:12 top choices with orthogonal corners, 56:56 total choices).

findings.consequent: Accuracy in choosing correct topology/floor plan (top choice)
findings.mechanism: Clipped corners made it more difficult for participants to gain a general understanding of the building.
findings.quote: participants who had experienced the clipped corners were less accurate in choosing the correct topology or the floor plan (15:13 for top choices, 64:48 for total choices)... x² = 3.90, p = .048 for top choices

findings.antecedent: Experienced environment with modified orthogonal conditions
findings.consequent: Accuracy in choosing correct topology/floor plan (top choice)
findings.mechanism: Orthogonal corners may facilitate a general understanding of the building's topology.
findings.quote: than were participants who had experienced the modified orthogonal conditions (22:6 for top choices, 83:19 for total choices), x² = 3.90, p = .048 for top choices

findings.consequent: Effect on choosing correct topology/floor plan
findings.quote: Alignment condition did not have any effect for this dimension.

findings.consequent: Preference for floor plans depicting elevator in upright orientation (top choice)
findings.mechanism: Participants in the aligned group preferred a plan that depicted the elevator in a square orientation.
findings.quote: significantly more participants in the aligned conditions chose floor plans depicting the elevator in an upright orientation as their top choice (20:8 as top choice, 58:54 for total choices)... This difference is significant for the top choices only, x² = 7.18, p = .007.

findings.consequent: Preference for floor plans depicting elevator in diamond orientation (rotated by 45°) (top choice)
findings.mechanism: The misaligned group preferred the elevator region to be in a diamond orientation (rotated by 45°).
findings.quote: Although participants in the aligned group preferred a plan that depicted the elevator in a square orientation, the misaligned group preferred the elevator region to be in a diamond orientation (rotated by 45°).

mechanisms: Misalignment of local reference frames impairs the integration of spatial knowledge across different parts of a building.
Increased cognitive workload due to the need to transform spatial information between misaligned reference frames.

The perceived spatial structure determines the selection of a reference frame aligned with this structure, and retrieval is more accurate when actual/imagined heading matches the main axis of the reference frame.
implementation_implications: Architectural design should ensure that the perceived spatial structure in each part of a building is encoded in aligned spatial reference frames, consistent with a global structure.
Buildings do not need to be organized around a simple orthogonal grid, but common axes should be made salient through symmetry, elongation, visual textures, or functional orientation.
Globally consistent frames of reference are beneficial for way-finding aids like 'you-are-here' maps.
Globally visible structures (atrium, outside landscape, prominent features) can provide a salient, global frame of reference to facilitate integration of different places.
limitations: The large range of individual way-finding times was partly a consequence of varying abilities of participants to navigate a synthetic environment with the mouse as a navigational interface.

The physical changes between clipped-corner and orthogonal-corner conditions (average length of hallways, ease of navigation around corners) might be responsible for observed differences, rather than just the corner type itself.

Participants were not very successful in correctly identifying the environment they had learned from the schematic floor plans, possibly due to the difficulty of matching immersive spatial experience to a 2D representation and the homogenous set of targets/distractors.
The alignment factor did not seem extraordinarily relevant for participants' conscious selections of a plan, implying they did not consciously attend to this feature.

The absolute orientation of the floor plan was arbitrary, and participants' preferences for one orientation merely indicate their cognitive preference for one orientation, not necessarily a direct effect of the alignment manipulation on their conscious choice.

paper_metadata.title: The Role of Spatial Reference Frames in Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_title: The Role of Spatial Reference Frames in Architecture
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: It is generally recognized that the spatial structure of a building is an important factor in way-finding performance. However, surprisingly little research has related way-finding performance directly to topological and geometrical properties of spatial environments. In this study, the authors provide empirical evidence that way-finding performance and the ability of people to orient themselves in their environment depends partly on geometrical relations between different parts of the space. The authors propose that the misalignment of local, cognitive reference frames suggested by architectural features leads to way-finding problems and impairs the integration of spatial knowledge. In an experiment with 56 participants, the authors tested way-finding performance and spatial memory for four virtual environments. Environments differed systematically in their alignment of parts of the building. Results show a main effect of alignment for both way-finding and pointing measures. Implications of these findings for both architectural design and cognitively motivated formal models of space are discussed.
